title: Hold the chariot (221–222)
hookLine: one who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot is a real driver; others only hold the reins
carry: other people are but holding the reins

cards: Anyone can hold a steering wheel. On an empty road on a sunny day, everyone's a fine driver.

The real test comes when a car cuts you off, or the road turns to ice, or the kid in the back seat spills the juice right as the light turns yellow. That's when you find out whether you're driving or just holding on.
Anger works the same way: everyone is patient when nothing is pushing. Chapter seventeen of the Dhammapada is about anger, and its second verse hands out a job title worth having.

teach.b: The chapter opens with verse two twenty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage!"
Then the image, verse two twenty-two: "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins."
Picture a chariot in the ancient world: horses at full gallop, wooden wheels, no brakes. Once it's rolling, stopping it takes real strength and skill. Anger, the verse says, is like that.
It arises, gathers speed, and wants to run.
Holding it back isn't the same as never feeling it. The skill is in not letting it run over anyone.

The Pali word for anger is kodha, and the verse's word for the real driver is sārathi, a charioteer: the same word Buddhists use in one of the Buddha's titles, the incomparable trainer of those who can be tamed.
The old commentary gives the verse a surprising story.
A monk, clearing ground for a hut, cut down a tree and injured the child of the spirit who lived in it. The tree spirit, furious, raised her hand to strike him. And then she stopped.
She held it back. She went to the Buddha and told him, and he praised her with this very verse. A real driver isn't the one who never feels the horses pull.
It's the one who feels them pull, hard, and still holds the chariot.

how: Buddhists practice restraining anger as it arises, by noticing it in the body, pausing and breathing, and many recite the Buddha's title 'the incomparable trainer of those who can be tamed' in daily chanting.

o: the reins a charioteer uses to steer
pride that makes you look down on others
anger, the heat that rises and wants to run

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: raised her hand, then held back

s: the verse says a real driver never feels anger at all
the chariot is already rolling: the skill is holding it back.
in the commentary, the one who held back anger was a tree spirit
a monk had injured her child, and she stopped herself from striking him.
verse 221 asks us to leave anger and forsake pride
"let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride."

games.q: you're a tree spirit. a monk has cut down your tree and hurt your child. your hand is raised to strike him. what do you do?
o: hold it back, and take it to the Buddha.
games.why: the commentary says she held back her anger and went to the Buddha, who praised her with this verse: a real driver.

practice: Remember a small moment of anger from this week, not the biggest one, and feel how it started: heat in the face, a tight jaw, words lining up. That's the chariot starting to roll.
Now, in your mind, take the reins, not by fighting the horses but by leaning back, slowing, one breath at a time, until you're the one driving.
